title: ADR: operator-observability-handoff-contract-2025
author: Maya Chen
content:
Summary
-------
This ADR defines a cross-team contract for handoff between service operators (teams that own runtime/infra components) and service authors (teams that ship features) focused on observability, telemetry enrichment, and runtime control signals. The goal is to reduce ambiguity in ownership for alerts, sampling, and feature flags that affect production behavior while preserving low-latency signal paths and bounded telemetry costs.

Context and motivation
----------------------
- Our platform runs many heterogeneous inference services and operators manage low-level runtime components (GPU schedulers, KV cache coordinator, prewarm agents, sidecars). Service authors implement business logic and model workflows.
- Past incidents have shown two recurring failure modes: (1) missing observability ownership on operator-managed signals (e.g., kernel preemption spikes), and (2) inconsistent enrichment of request context across the call path causing sparse traces and noisy alerts.
- We need a clear, minimal contract to ensure operator signals are actionable, traceable back to service owners, and that any operator-initiated control (throttles, evictions, degradation) includes deterministic metadata for triage and cost accounting.

Decision
--------
We adopt a lightweight "operator observability handoff" contract with the following rules:

1) Signal classification and ownership
   - Operators must publish a documented signal catalog with: signal id, type (gauge/counter/event/trace-span), cardinality expectation, SLO/relevance tier, suggested alert thresholds, and primary owner (team).
   - Service teams consuming these signals must include the operator signal id in their incident runbooks and subscribe to the corresponding alerting channel.

2) Enrichment envelope
   - Every operator-generated event or trace span must include a standardized enrichment envelope with the following required fields: environment, service_id, instance_id, operator_component, operator_action, request_id (if applicable), sample_rate_hint. Optional fields are user_tenant, model_variant, and cost_tags.
   - Example JSON envelope (short):
     {
       "operator_component": "kv-evictor",
       "operator_action": "evict",
       "service_id": "content-synth-service",
       "instance_id": "kv-evictor-3",
       "request_id": "req-1234abcd",
       "sample_rate_hint": "0.05"
     }

3) Sampling and budget hints
   - Operators must include a sample_rate_hint on high-cardinality signals. This is advisory but required in the catalog. The default global cap for operator signal ingestion is 10% of request traces; operators must design for sub-1% sampling for high-cardinality metadata unless approved by SRE.

4) Open telemetry path and low-latency controls
   - Operator telemetry MUST use the shared tracing header (x-rw-trace) to preserve parent-child relationships across RPC boundaries. If a request lacks a trace header, operators must attach a synthetic span with reason="orphaned".
   - Control-plane actions (throttles/evictions) must emit both an event and a trace span within 2s of the action to avoid blind spots in triage pipelines.

5) Alerting and remediation playbooks
   - Operators provide a default alert definition with suggested thresholds and a short remediation checklist (3–5 steps). Service owners are responsible for validating and adapting thresholds as part of their SLA gating.

6) Change management and schema evolution
   - Any change to the enrichment envelope schema or signal catalog requires a two-week review window and an automated compatibility test that validates presence/absence tolerances. Backwards-compatible additions are allowed; removals must be announced and feature-flagged.

Rationale
---------
- Clear signal ownership prevents alert ping-pong between teams.
- Standardized enrichment ensures traces/events can be automatically correlated to requests, models, and cost buckets.
- Sampling guidance constrains telemetry cost growth without removing operator visibility.
- Fast emission of control-plane traces reduces MTTI in incidents where operators trigger runtime degradation.

Consequences and tradeoffs
-------------------------
- Pros: Faster triage, better SLO root cause mapping, bounded telemetry costs, clearer on-call responsibilities.
- Cons: Slight increase in operator implementation burden to include enrichment and catalog maintenance. Potential for initial false positives if thresholds are not tuned by service owners.

Rollout plan and checklist (recommended)
----------------------------------------
1) Pilot (2 teams, 4 weeks)\   - Choose two operator components (kv-evictor and prewarm-agent) and two service owners.\   - Implement enrichment envelope and add entries to the signal catalog.\   - Run compatibility tests and simulate synthetic traffic to validate sampling.
2) Stage rollout (8 weeks)\   - Gate: operator health and zero regressions on telemetry pipeline.\   - Add alert definitions to the monitoring workspace and confirm on-call notifications.
3) GA (4 weeks)\   - All new operator features must comply with the contract.\   - Produce a short training session and update runbooks.

Operational requirements and SLO mapping
--------------------------------------
| Item | Owner | SLO / Target | Notes |
|------|-------|--------------|-------|
| Signal catalog availability | Operator team | 99.9% doc access | Catalog hosted in Confluence + versioned YAML in git |
| Control trace emission latency | Operator team | 95% < 2s | Measured from action to span emitted |
| Enrichment completeness | Service & operator teams | 99% required fields present | Validated by CI lint step |

Compatibility examples and CLI snippets
--------------------------------------
- Linting command (pre-commit hook):
  rw-telemetry-lint --file operator-events.yaml --schema schemas/envelope-v1.json

- Example YAML catalog entry:
  - id: op.kv.evict
    type: event
    cardinality: high
    sample_rate_hint: 0.01
    owner: infra-kv
    alert: infra-kv.eviction-rate.p95 > 10/min

- Quick test to emit a control trace span (dev cluster):
  curl -X POST https://dev-telemetry.rw.internal/emit -d '{"operator_component":"kv-evictor","operator_action":"evict","service_id":"content-synth-service","request_id":"test-req"}'

Ownership and governance
------------------------
- Operator teams: maintain signal catalog, implement envelope, and create initial alerting prototypes.
- Service teams: adapt runbooks, validate thresholds, and own final alert ownership.
- SRE: review sampling budgets quarterly and adjudicate exceptions.
- Observability platform: provide linting/validation hooks in CI and a lightweight dashboard to visualize operator signal ingestion rates.

Open questions and future work
-----------------------------
- How do we attach cost attribution to operator actions at sub-request granularity for mixed-tenant workloads? Proposal: extend cost_tags with tenant_id and model_variant; track in a separate billing pipeline.
- Can we unify sample_rate_hint into a dynamic feedback mechanism that increases sampling during incidents? Future work: short experiment with adaptive sampling controller.

Appendix: example validation rule (pseudo-YAML)
------------------------------------------------
- name: envelope-required-fields
  check: all_required_fields_present
  required_fields: [operator_component, operator_action, service_id, instance_id]
  severity: error
